\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The phenomenon}
Newtonian gravitation is false, and it is used to navigate spacecraft. The Bohr
model is false, and it reproduces the hydrogen spectrum to four significant
figures. The ideal gas law is false, and it designs refrigerators. Every
truncated loop expansion in quantum field theory is false \emph{by construction}
--- its author can name the infinitely many terms discarded --- and such
truncations constitute essentially all of the quantitative predictive content of
the Standard Model.

The pattern is so pervasive that it has become a proverb (``all models are wrong,
but some are useful'') rather than an object of study. Our aim is to make it an
object of study: to identify a class of approximately correct theories, define
predictive superiority precisely, and prove theorems delimiting exactly when and
where an acknowledged falsehood outperforms its rivals.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item A definition of a perturbative family of theories with a uniform Cauchy
bound, and quantitative convergence of the associated wrongness series
(\S\ref{sec:core}).
\item The meta-theorem on the unreasonable effectiveness of wrong theories, with
the strong quantifier order in which the coupling window precedes the choice of
rival, together with nonemptiness and genericity results (\S\ref{sec:meta}).
\item Structural results on comparative adequacy: the epistemic half-space
theorem, the Condorcet obstruction, optimality of every theory in some world, and
the compatibility of universal falsity with uniform convergence
(\S\ref{sec:structure}).
\item The wrongness hierarchy: two-sided tail estimates and the strict ordering
of the tower of truncations (\S\ref{sec:hierarchy}).
\item Sharpness: explicit counterexamples showing both main theorems fail outside
their windows (\S\ref{sec:sharp}).
\item A worked instance from critical phenomena (\S\ref{sec:wilson}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Perturbative theory-space and the wrongness series}\label{sec:core}

Throughout, $\Ph$ is an arbitrary set whose elements are called \emph{phenomena}.
No structure on $\Ph$ is assumed.

\begin{definition}[Theory]
A \emph{theory} on $\Ph$ is a function $T:\Ph\to\R$; $T(p)$ is the numerical
prediction for the measurable quantity $p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Perturbative family]\label{def:pert}
A \emph{perturbative family of theories} over $\Ph$ consists of a \emph{truth}
function $t:\Ph\to\R$, correction coefficients $a_n:\Ph\to\R$ for $n\in\N$, and
constants $B\ge 0$ (the \emph{bound}) and $r\ge0$ (the \emph{ratio}), subject to
the uniform Cauchy estimate
\[
  |a_n(p)| \;\le\; B\,r^{\,n}\qquad\text{for all }n\in\N,\ p\in\Ph.
\]
\end{definition}

The estimate is the classical Cauchy bound for the Taylor coefficients of a
function analytic in a disc of radius $1/r$, imposed \emph{uniformly in the
phenomenon}. A perturbative family is thus a germ of an analytic deformation of
the truth with $p$ as a spectator parameter.

\begin{definition}[Wrongness, prediction, truncation]
For a perturbative family, a coupling $\eps\in\R$ and a phenomenon $p$, put
\[
  w_n(\eps,p)=a_n(p)\,\eps^{\,n+1},\qquad
  W(\eps,p)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}w_n(\eps,p),
\]
\[
  T_\eps(p)=t(p)+W(\eps,p),\qquad
  T^{(N)}_\eps(p)=t(p)+\sum_{n<N}w_n(\eps,p).
\]
The quantity $W(\eps,p)$ is the \emph{wrongness}; by construction
$T_\eps(p)-t(p)=W(\eps,p)$.
\end{definition}

The series begins at $\eps^{1}$: at zero coupling the family is exactly true.

\begin{definition}[Error and superiority]
For theories $T,C$ and truth $t$ the \emph{prediction error} is
$E(T,p)=|T(p)-t(p)|$. We say $T$ \emph{beats} $C$ at $p$, written
$T\succ_p C$, if $E(T,p)<E(C,p)$. The \emph{superiority region} is
$\Sup(T,C)=\{p\in\Ph: T\succ_p C\}$.
\end{definition}

Superiority is irreflexive and asymmetric, being the pullback of the strict order
on $\R$ along the error map. It is \emph{not} aggregable into a transitive global
relation; see \S\ref{sec:condorcet}.

\subsection{Convergence}

\begin{lemma}[Termwise geometric domination]\label{lem:dom}
$|w_n(\eps,p)|\le (B|\eps|)\,(r|\eps|)^n$ for all $n,p,\eps$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$|w_n|=|a_n(p)|\,|\eps|^{n+1}\le Br^n|\eps|^{n+1}=(B|\eps|)(r|\eps|)^n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}
If $r|\eps|<1$ then $\sum_n w_n(\eps,p)$ converges absolutely for every $p$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Comparison with the geometric series $\sum_n (B|\eps|)(r|\eps|)^n$ via
Lemma~\ref{lem:dom}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative convergence of wrongness]\label{thm:cauchy}
For $r|\eps|<1$ and every $p\in\Ph$,
\[
  |W(\eps,p)|\;\le\;\frac{B\,|\eps|}{1-r|\eps|}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By the triangle inequality for absolutely convergent series
$|W|\le\sum_n|w_n|$; by Lemma~\ref{lem:dom} and termwise comparison this is at
most $\sum_n (B|\eps|)(r|\eps|)^n = B|\eps|/(1-r|\eps|)$.
\end{proof}

The right-hand side contains no reference to $p$: the bound is uniform over the
entire space of phenomena.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform smallness of wrongness]\label{thm:small}
For every $\eta>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ with
\[
  |\eps|<\delta \;\Longrightarrow\; |W(\eps,p)|<\eta \ \text{ for all } p\in\Ph,
\]
and one may take
\[
  \delta=\min\left\{\frac{1}{2(r+1)},\ \frac{\eta}{2(B+1)}\right\}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first entry forces $r|\eps|\le 1/2$, hence $1-r|\eps|\ge 1/2$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:cauchy} gives $|W|\le 2B|\eps|$. The second forces
$(B+1)|\eps|<\eta/2$, hence $2B|\eps|<\eta$. The additive $+1$'s keep the
expressions positive in the degenerate cases $B=0$ or $r=0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Asymptotic order of truncations}

\begin{definition}
A function $f:\R\to\R$ \emph{vanishes to order $k$ at zero} if there are $C>0$
and $\delta>0$ with $|f(\eps)|\le C|\eps|^k$ whenever $|\eps|<\delta$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Tail bound]\label{lem:tailbound}
For $r|\eps|<1$,
\[
  \Big|W(\eps,p)-\sum_{n<N}w_n(\eps,p)\Big|
   \;\le\; \frac{B\,|\eps|^{N+1}r^{N}}{1-r|\eps|}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Split off the first $N$ terms; the remainder is $\sum_{m\ge0}w_{m+N}$, and
\[
  |w_{m+N}|\;\le\;\big(B|\eps|^{N+1}r^{N}\big)\,(r|\eps|)^{m}.
\]
Summing the geometric majorant gives the bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Order of the truncation error]
For every $p$ and $N$, the map $\eps\mapsto T_\eps(p)-T^{(N)}_\eps(p)$ vanishes
to order $N+1$ at zero; explicitly, for $|\eps|<1/(2(r+1))$,
\[
  \big|T_\eps(p)-T^{(N)}_\eps(p)\big| \;\le\; 2(B+1)(r+1)^N|\eps|^{N+1}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The window forces $1-r|\eps|\ge 1/2$; feed this into Lemma~\ref{lem:tailbound}
and enlarge $Br^N$ to $(B+1)(r+1)^N$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Linear structure}
Perturbative families may be added and rescaled: $T\oplus S$ adds truths and
coefficients, with bound $B_T+B_S$ and ratio $\max(r_T,r_S)$ (the Cauchy estimate
survives since $r_T^n,r_S^n\le\max(r_T,r_S)^n$); and $c\odot T$ scales truth and
coefficients, with bound $|c|B_T$ and the same ratio.

\begin{proposition}[Linearity of wrongness]
If $r_T|\eps|<1$ and $r_S|\eps|<1$ then
$W_{T\oplus S}=W_T+W_S$ and $(T\oplus S)_\eps=T_\eps+S_\eps$; and for any
$c\in\R$, $W_{c\odot T}=c\,W_T$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Termwise identities together with additivity and homogeneity of absolutely
convergent sums.
\end{proof}

\section{The meta-theorem}\label{sec:meta}

\begin{theorem}[Unreasonable effectiveness of wrong theories]\label{thm:meta}
Let $T$ be a perturbative family with truth $t$ and let $\eta>0$. Then there is
$\delta>0$ such that for every coupling $\eps$ with $|\eps|<\delta$, every theory
$C:\Ph\to\R$, and every phenomenon $p$ with $E(C,p)\ge\eta$,
\[
  T_\eps \succ_p C .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $\delta$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:small} for the tolerance $\eta$. For
$|\eps|<\delta$,
$E(T_\eps,p)=|T_\eps(p)-t(p)|=|W(\eps,p)|<\eta\le E(C,p)$.
\end{proof}

The proof is short; the content is in the quantifier order. The window $\delta$
is produced \emph{before} the competitor $C$ and the phenomenon $p$ are named,
and depends only on the internal data $(B,r)$ of the approximate theory and on
$\eta$. A single window works simultaneously against \emph{all} theories on
$\Ph$.

\begin{remark}
The theorem does not claim $T_\eps$ is true (generically $W(\eps,p)\ne0$), nor
that it beats $C$ everywhere. It says exactly that the region of $C$'s badness is
a region of $T_\eps$'s comparative goodness.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[Bad sets are superiority regions]
For every $\eta>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that for all $|\eps|<\delta$ and all
theories $C$, $\{p: E(C,p)\ge\eta\}\subseteq \Sup(T_\eps,C)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Nonempty superiority region]\label{cor:nonempty}
If $C(p_0)\ne t(p_0)$ for some $p_0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that
$\Sup(T_\eps,C)\ne\emptyset$ for all $|\eps|<\delta$; indeed
$p_0\in\Sup(T_\eps,C)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:meta} with $\eta=E(C,p_0)>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Genericity of nowhere-exactness]\label{thm:generic}
Let $\Ph$ be countable, $T$ any theory, $t$ any truth, and $\delta>0$. Then there
is $c$ with $0<c<\delta$ such that $T(p)+c\ne t(p)$ for every $p\in\Ph$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The set $\mathcal B=\{t(p)-T(p): p\in\Ph\}$ of bad shifts is the image of a
countable set, hence countable, while $(0,\delta)$ has the cardinality of the
continuum and is therefore not contained in $\mathcal B$. Any
$c\in(0,\delta)\setminus\mathcal B$ works.
\end{proof}

Thus an arbitrarily small perturbation makes any theory wrong at every
phenomenon: the nowhere-exact theories are dense, and so the hypothesis
appearing in Corollary~\ref{cor:nonempty} describes the typical case rather
than an exceptional one.

\begin{proposition}[Disagreement forces error]
For any theories $T,C$, any truth $t$, and any $p$,
$|T(p)-C(p)|\le E(T,p)+E(C,p)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
$T(p)-C(p)=(T(p)-t(p))-(C(p)-t(p))$; apply the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

Contrapositively: if two theories disagree by $D$ at a phenomenon then, whatever
the truth, at least one errs by at least $D/2$ there. Controversy is a
truth-independent lower bound on collective ignorance.

\section{The structure of comparative adequacy}\label{sec:structure}

\subsection{The epistemic half-space theorem}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:half}
For all $a,b,t\in\R$: $\;|t-a|<|t-b| \iff (b-a)(2t-a-b)<0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Both sides of the first inequality are nonnegative, so it is equivalent to
$(t-a)^2<(t-b)^2$; expanding and rearranging gives $(b-a)(2t-a-b)<0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Epistemic half-space theorem]\label{thm:halfspace}
For $a\ne b$ the set of worlds
$\mathcal W(a\succ b)=\{t\in\R: |t-a|<|t-b|\}$
is open, contains $a$, and is unbounded: for every $M$ there is
$t\in\mathcal W(a\succ b)$ with $|t|>M$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:half} the set is $\{t:(b-a)(2t-a-b)<0\}$, the preimage of the
open ray $(-\infty,0)$ under a nonconstant affine map, hence an open half-line.
It contains $t=a$ since $0=|a-a|<|a-b|$. If $a<b$ the half-line is
$t<(a+b)/2$, unbounded below; if $b<a$ it is $t>(a+b)/2$, unbounded above. Either
way witnesses of arbitrarily large modulus exist.
\end{proof}

Predictive inferiority is therefore never intrinsic to a theory: any theory
making a definite prediction is optimal in an unbounded open family of worlds.

\begin{theorem}[Every theory is optimal in some world]
Let $(F_i)_{i\in I}$ be theories and $p$ a phenomenon with $F_j(p)\ne F_i(p)$ for
all $j\ne i$. Then there is a truth $t$ with $F_i\succ_p F_j$ for every $j\ne i$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take $t=F_i$: then $E(F_i,p)=0$ while $E(F_j,p)=|F_j(p)-F_i(p)|>0$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Condorcet obstruction}\label{sec:condorcet}

Say $X$ \emph{majority-beats} $Y$ if $X$ beats $Y$ on a majority of phenomena.

\begin{theorem}[Condorcet cycle in theory-space]\label{thm:condorcet}
Let $\Ph=\{p_1,p_2,p_3\}$, let the truth be $t\equiv0$, and let
\[
  A=(1,2,3),\qquad B=(2,3,1),\qquad C=(3,1,2)
\]
(the predictions, hence also the errors, at $p_1,p_2,p_3$). Then $A$
majority-beats $B$, $B$ majority-beats $C$, and $C$ majority-beats $A$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$A$ beats $B$ at $p_1$ ($1<2$) and $p_2$ ($2<3$); $B$ beats $C$ at $p_1$ ($2<3$)
and $p_3$ ($1<2$); $C$ beats $A$ at $p_2$ ($1<2$) and $p_3$ ($2<3$). Each is a
two-out-of-three majority.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}
$A$ does not majority-beat $C$: it wins only at $p_1$ ($1<3$), losing at $p_2$
($2>1$) and $p_3$ ($3>2$).
\end{proposition}

\begin{corollary}[Non-transitivity of empirical adequacy]
Majority empirical adequacy is not transitive; in particular it is not a preorder,
and there is no linear ordering of theories by ``closeness to truth'' compatible
with majority comparison over phenomena.
\end{corollary}

This is an obstruction of Arrovian type: any aggregation of pointwise errors into
a total order on theory-space must sacrifice transitivity or independence of the
phenomena. Comparative adequacy should be modelled as a \emph{directed graph} on
theory-space, with cycles permitted. Theorem~\ref{thm:meta} escapes the
obstruction precisely because it never aggregates.

\subsection{Universal falsity is compatible with convergence}

\begin{theorem}[Meta-induction is compatible with convergence]\label{thm:pmi}
For any truth $t:\Ph\to\R$ there is a sequence of theories $(F_k)_{k\in\N}$ with
\begin{enumerate}
\item $F_k(p)\ne t(p)$ for \emph{every} $k$ and \emph{every} $p$; and
\item uniform convergence of errors: for every $\eta>0$ there is $K$ with
$E(F_k,p)<\eta$ for all $k\ge K$ and all $p$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take $F_k=t+\frac{1}{k+1}$. Then $E(F_k,p)=\frac1{k+1}>0$ for all $p$, giving
(1); and given $\eta>0$ choose $K>1/\eta$, so that $\frac1{k+1}<\frac1K<\eta$ for
$k\ge K$, giving (2).
\end{proof}

The \emph{pessimistic meta-induction} infers from the falsity of all past
theories that present theories should not be believed.
Theorem~\ref{thm:pmi} shows the inference from ``all false'' to ``no
convergence'' is invalid: falsity is a binary predicate, approximate correctness
is a magnitude, and the argument conflates them.

\section{The wrongness hierarchy}\label{sec:hierarchy}

Physicists do not sum perturbation series; they truncate them. We ask whether the
tower $T^{(0)}_\eps, T^{(1)}_\eps, T^{(2)}_\eps,\dots$ is ordered by predictive
accuracy relative to the exact prediction $T_\eps$.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{$N$-th tail} is
$R_N(\eps,p)=W(\eps,p)-\sum_{n<N}w_n(\eps,p)$: the part of the correction
discarded by the $N$-th truncation.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Truncation error is the tail]\label{lem:trunc}
Measuring error against the exact prediction $T_\eps$,
$E\big(T^{(N)}_\eps,p\big)=|R_N(\eps,p)|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$T^{(N)}_\eps(p)-T_\eps(p)=-R_N(\eps,p)$; take absolute values.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tail recursion]\label{lem:rec}
$R_N = w_N + R_{N+1}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Immediate from $\sum_{n<N+1}=\sum_{n<N}+w_N$.
\end{proof}

The recursion is the whole mechanism: the error of a truncation is its first
neglected term plus the error of the next truncation.

\begin{proposition}[Two-sided tail estimates]\label{prop:twosided}
Suppose $r|\eps|\le 1/2$. Then
\[
  |a_N(p)|\,|\eps|^{N+1}-2B\,r^{N+1}|\eps|^{N+2}
  \;\le\; |R_N(\eps,p)| \;\le\; 2B\,r^{N}|\eps|^{N+1}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Upper: Lemma~\ref{lem:tailbound} with $1-r|\eps|\ge 1/2$. Lower: by
Lemma~\ref{lem:rec}, $|w_N|=|R_N-R_{N+1}|\le|R_N|+|R_{N+1}|$, so
$|R_N|\ge |w_N|-|R_{N+1}|\ge |a_N(p)||\eps|^{N+1}-2Br^{N+1}|\eps|^{N+2}$, using
the upper bound at order $N+1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Wrongness hierarchy theorem]\label{thm:hierarchy}
Let $p$ satisfy $a_M(p)\ne0$ and let $N>M$. Then there is $\delta>0$ such that
for every $\eps$ with $0<|\eps|<\delta$,
\[
  E\big(T^{(N)}_\eps,p\big) \;<\; E\big(T^{(M)}_\eps,p\big),
\]
errors being measured against the exact prediction $T_\eps$. One may take
\[
  \delta=\min\left\{1,\ \frac{1}{2(r+1)},\
  \frac{c}{2B\,(r^{N}+r^{M+1})+1}\right\},\qquad c=|a_M(p)| .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first two entries put the coupling in the half-disc $r|\eps|\le 1/2$ and
ensure $|\eps|<1$, so $|\eps|^{N+1}\le|\eps|^{M+2}$ since $N+1\ge M+2$. The third
gives the decisive linear inequality
$|\eps|\cdot 2B(r^{N}+r^{M+1})<c$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:twosided} the finer truncation obeys
$|R_N|\le 2Br^N|\eps|^{N+1}\le 2Br^N|\eps|^{M+2}$ and the coarser one obeys
$|R_M|\ge c|\eps|^{M+1}-2Br^{M+1}|\eps|^{M+2}$. It therefore suffices that
\[
  2Br^{N}|\eps|^{M+2} \;<\; c|\eps|^{M+1}-2Br^{M+1}|\eps|^{M+2},
\]
which after division by $|\eps|^{M+1}>0$ is exactly the decisive inequality. The
conclusion follows with Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc}.
\end{proof}

Up to the harmless $+1$ regularisers, $\delta$ is the ratio of the \emph{signal}
--- the first term the coarse theory neglects --- to the \emph{noise}, the
geometric mass of what both theories neglect. Higher order improves prediction
exactly while the newly captured term outweighs everything still missing.

\begin{theorem}[Uniform window for consecutive steps]\label{thm:consecutive}
Let $K\in\N$ and suppose $a_M(p)\ne0$ for all $M<K$. Then there is a single
$\delta>0$ such that for all $0<|\eps|<\delta$ and all $M<K$,
$E\big(T^{(M+1)}_\eps,p\big)<E\big(T^{(M)}_\eps,p\big)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Induction on $K$, taking at each stage the minimum of the inductively obtained
window and the window supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:hierarchy} for the step $M=K$;
finitely many minima remain positive.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The tower is totally ordered]\label{thm:chain}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:consecutive} there is a single
$\delta>0$ such that for all $0<|\eps|<\delta$ and all $M<N\le K$,
\[
  E\big(T^{(N)}_\eps,p\big)<E\big(T^{(M)}_\eps,p\big).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Induction on $N$ using Theorem~\ref{thm:consecutive} and transitivity of $<$.
\end{proof}

Convergence alone (Theorem~\ref{thm:small}) says only that the limit is right.
Theorem~\ref{thm:chain} says the approach is strictly monotone in the order of
approximation, on one common window: the successive knowing falsehoods of the
perturbative tower are linearly ordered by empirical adequacy. Note that
$\eps=0$ must be excluded, since there every truncation is exactly correct.

\section{Sharpness: the windows are real}\label{sec:sharp}

The counterexamples use the \emph{binomial family}: over a one-point phenomenon
space with truth $0$, take $a_0=\alpha$, $a_1=\beta$ and $a_n=0$ for $n\ge2$,
with $B=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ and $r=1$. Its wrongness series terminates:
$W(\eps)=\alpha\eps+\beta\eps^2$.

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the meta-theorem]\label{thm:sharpmeta}
There exist a perturbative family $T$, a coupling $\eps$, a rival $C$ and a
phenomenon $p$ such that $C(p)\ne t(p)$ --- so $C$ is itself wrong --- and yet
$T_\eps$ does \emph{not} beat $C$ at $p$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take the binomial family with $\alpha=1,\beta=0$, so $T_\eps=\eps$ around the
truth $0$; take $C\equiv 1/4$ and $\eps=1/2$. Then $E(T_{1/2})=1/2$ while
$E(C)=1/4<1/2$.
\end{proof}

At a coupling of size $1/2$ an approximately correct theory is beaten by a crude
constant guess with no theoretical warrant. The conclusion of
Theorem~\ref{thm:meta} therefore genuinely fails without its window: a
perturbative calculation pushed to strong coupling can be worse than a rough
phenomenological guess.

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness of the hierarchy theorem]\label{thm:sharphier}
There exist a perturbative family $T$, a coupling $\eps$ and a phenomenon $p$
with $a_0(p)\ne0$ such that
$E\big(T^{(0)}_\eps,p\big)<E\big(T^{(1)}_\eps,p\big)$: the higher truncation is
strictly worse.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take the binomial family with $\alpha=1,\beta=-3$, so $W(\eps)=\eps-3\eps^2$, and
set $\eps=1$. Then $R_0=W(1)=-2$ and $R_1=W(1)-a_0\eps=-3$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:trunc} the errors are $2$ and $3$ respectively.
\end{proof}

Adding a correction made the prediction worse, so Theorem~\ref{thm:hierarchy}
cannot be upgraded to a global statement: monotone improvement along the tower is
a genuinely small-coupling phenomenon, exactly as in strongly coupled regimes and
in divergent asymptotic series generally.

Both failures share the shape \emph{true inside a window, false outside it}, with
the window explicit and computable from $(B,r,\eta)$ or
$(B,r,|a_M(p)|,N,M)$. The framework is thus a criterion, not merely an apologia.

\section{Worked instance: the two-loop $\eps$-expansion}\label{sec:wilson}

In the Wilson--Fisher analysis of critical phenomena one studies scalar field
theory in $d=4-\eps$ dimensions; the interacting fixed point of the
renormalisation-group flow occurs at a coupling of order $\eps$, and the
anomalous dimension of the field there is, at two loops,
\[
  \eta(\eps)=\frac{\eps^2}{54}+O(\eps^3).
\]
Viewed as a perturbative family over a one-point phenomenon space with truth $0$
this is exactly the binomial family with $a_0=0$, $a_1=1/54$:
$W(\eps)=\tfrac{1}{54}\eps^2=\eta(\eps)$.

\begin{theorem}[The meta-theorem for the $\eps$-expansion]
For every accuracy threshold $\eta_0>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that for every
$\eps$ with $|\eps|<\delta$ and every rival theory $C$ whose error exceeds
$\eta_0$, the two-loop prediction $\eps^2/54$ beats $C$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Immediate from Theorem~\ref{thm:meta} applied to the family above, after
identifying $T_\eps$ with $\eps\mapsto\eps^2/54$.
\end{proof}

Three observations. The two-loop formula \emph{is} a knowingly wrong theory:
infinitely many terms are discarded and the full series is believed divergent.
The meta-theorem nonetheless certifies its superiority over all
sufficiently-inaccurate rivals in a window near four dimensions. And the
physically interesting case $\eps=1$ (three dimensions) is \emph{not} inside any
small window: that the extrapolated formula still yields critical exponents
accurate to a few percent for real fluids and magnets is good fortune the present
theorems neither explain nor claim to.

\section{Algorithms}

Every window above is a closed-form expression in the data.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Window for the meta-theorem.} Input $B,r,\eta$; output
$\delta=\min\{1/(2(r+1)),\ \eta/(2(B+1))\}$, in $O(1)$ arithmetic operations.
Correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:small}.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Window for the hierarchy.} Input $B,r,c=|a_M(p)|$ and orders
$M<N$; output
$\delta=\min\{1,\ 1/(2(r+1)),\ c/(2B(r^{N}+r^{M+1})+1)\}$, in $O(\log N)$ by fast
exponentiation. For a chain $0,\dots,K$ take the minimum over consecutive steps,
$O(K\log K)$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Superiority-region certification.} Given finitely many phenomena
with rival predictions and truths, and a threshold $\eta$, the certified subset is
$\{p:|C(p)-t(p)|\ge\eta\}$, computable in $O(|\Ph|)$ evaluations \emph{without
evaluating the approximate theory at all} --- the meta-theorem does the work.
Comparing with the actual superiority region quantifies how conservative the
certificate is.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What the framework explains}
\emph{Uniformity.} The Cauchy bound is uniform in the phenomenon, so accuracy is
bought across the whole domain of application at once; this is why the window can
precede the rival, and why an approximate theory functions as a general-purpose
instrument.
\emph{Locality of comparison.} Superiority is pointwise; the meta-theorem claims
dominance only where the rival is bad, side-stepping the Condorcet obstruction.
\emph{Order structure of truncation.} The tail recursion organises deliberate
falsehoods into a strictly improving chain, which is why ``compute one more
order'' is a rational strategy despite every order being wrong.

\subsection{Limitations}
The Cauchy bound excludes the asymptotic series with factorially growing
coefficients, $|a_n|\sim n!\,r^n$, ubiquitous in quantum field theory; for these
there is no radius of convergence and the tower cannot improve forever. The error
functional is the absolute pointwise deviation; realistic comparisons weight
phenomena by experimental precision and involve vector-valued predictions (the
half-space theorem generalises to hyperplane bisectors; the Condorcet obstruction
can only worsen). Finally, the framework addresses predictive accuracy alone and
says nothing about explanation, unification or ontological correctness.

\subsection{Relation to philosophy of science}
Three classical positions acquire precise counterparts. \emph{Instrumentalism}:
the meta-theorem certifies performance while remaining silent on truth.
\emph{Convergent realism}: Theorems~\ref{thm:small} and~\ref{thm:chain} supply the
convergence it needs without requiring any theory to be true. \emph{The
pessimistic meta-induction}: Theorem~\ref{thm:pmi} invalidates the inference from
universal past falsity to non-convergence. Theorem~\ref{thm:halfspace} adds a
fourth: appraisal of a theory is irreducibly a joint appraisal of theory and
world.

\section{Future work}

\begin{conjecture}[Optimal truncation in the asymptotic regime]
For families with only a factorially divergent bound $|a_n|\le B\,n!\,r^n$ there
is a truncation order $N^*(\eps)\asymp 1/(r|\eps|)$ such that $T^{(N^*)}_\eps$
beats every truncation of order $N\ne N^*(\eps)$, with error exponentially small,
$O(\exp(-1/(r|\eps|)))$.
\end{conjecture}
The mechanism is already visible: the decisive inequality in
Theorem~\ref{thm:hierarchy} reverses once coefficient growth beats geometric
decay, so the strict chain of Theorem~\ref{thm:chain} must \emph{terminate} at a
computable order. The two-sided estimates of Proposition~\ref{prop:twosided} hold
for arbitrary coefficient bounds; only the geometric majorant needs replacing.

\begin{conjecture}[Measure-theoretic effectiveness]
Equip the space of worlds (truth functions on a phenomenon set of size $k$) with
Lebesgue measure on a bounded box. For any two distinct theories the set of
worlds in which one majority-beats the other has strictly positive measure, and
for odd $k$ the two majority regions have measures summing to the total.
\end{conjecture}
Theorem~\ref{thm:halfspace} already exhibits each pointwise favouring set as an
open half-line, so each majority region is a finite union of intersections of
half-spaces --- a polyhedral set with computable measure.

Further directions: a tournament-theoretic semantics for comparative adequacy
(which tournaments arise from error profiles; the distribution of cycle lengths;
whether Copeland- or Kemeny-style scores admit a canonical justification); and the
use of explicit windows as a research heuristic, computing from estimated Cauchy
data the coupling range in which the next order is guaranteed to help.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core objects
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class PerturbativeFamily:
    """A perturbative family of theories over a finite phenomenon set.

    Attributes
    ----------
    truth : mapping phenomenon -> exact value.
    coeff : coefficient function (n, p) -> a_n(p); the coefficient of
            eps^(n+1) in the wrongness series.
    bound : constant B with |a_n(p)| <= B r^n for all n, p.
    ratio : constant r (inverse radius of convergence).
    n_max : practical truncation used for numerically summing the series.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        truth: Callable[[str], float],
        coeff: Callable[[int, str], float],
        bound: float,
        ratio: float,
        n_max: int = 400,
        terminating: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        if bound < 0.0 or ratio < 0.0:
            raise ValueError("bound and ratio must be nonnegative")
        self.truth = truth
        self.coeff = coeff
        self.bound = bound
        self.ratio = ratio
        self.n_max = n_max
        # A terminating series (finitely many nonzero coefficients) converges
        # for every coupling, so the disc-of-convergence guard is waived.
        self.terminating = terminating

    # -- series -----------------------------------------------------------

    def term(self, n: int, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """The n-th term a_n(p) eps^(n+1) of the wrongness series."""
        return self.coeff(n, p) * eps ** (n + 1)

    def wrongness(self, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """W(eps, p): the total deviation of the theory from the truth."""
        if not self.terminating and self.ratio * abs(eps) >= 1.0:
            raise ValueError("outside the disc of convergence: r|eps| >= 1")
        return math.fsum(self.term(n, eps, p) for n in range(self.n_max))

    def predict(self, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """The exact prediction truth(p) + W(eps, p)."""
        return self.truth(p) + self.wrongness(eps, p)

    def truncate(self, order: int, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """The order-N truncation: keep n < N, discard the rest."""
        return self.truth(p) + math.fsum(
            self.term(n, eps, p) for n in range(order)
        )

    def tail(self, order: int, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """R_N = W - sum_{n<N} w_n: exactly what the truncation throws away."""
        return self.wrongness(eps, p) - math.fsum(
            self.term(n, eps, p) for n in range(order)
        )

    # -- certified bounds and windows -------------------------------------

    def cauchy_bound(self, eps: float) -> float:
        """The uniform estimate B|eps| / (1 - r|eps|) on |W(eps, p)|."""
        denom = 1.0 - self.ratio * abs(eps)
        if denom <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError("outside the disc of convergence")
        return self.bound * abs(eps) / denom

    def meta_window(self, eta: float) -> float:
        """delta such that |eps| < delta implies |W(eps,p)| < eta for all p."""
        if eta <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError("threshold eta must be positive")
        return min(
            1.0 / (2.0 * (self.ratio + 1.0)),
            eta / (2.0 * (self.bound + 1.0)),
        )

    def hierarchy_window(self, m: int, n: int, p: str) -> float:
        """delta such that 0<|eps|<delta implies order-n beats order-m at p."""
        if not m < n:
            raise ValueError("require m < n")
        c = abs(self.coeff(m, p))
        if c == 0.0:
            raise ValueError("the m-th correction vanishes at p")
        noise = 2.0 * self.bound * (self.ratio ** n + self.ratio ** (m + 1)) + 1.0
        return min(1.0, 1.0 / (2.0 * (self.ratio + 1.0)), c / noise)


def pred_err(value: float, truth_value: float) -> float:
    """Pointwise prediction error |value - truth|."""
    return abs(value - truth_value)


def beats(value_a: float, value_b: float, truth_value: float) -> bool:
    """Does prediction a land strictly closer to the truth than b?"""
    return pred_err(value_a, truth_value) < pred_err(value_b, truth_value)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Concrete families
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def binomial_family(a0: float, a1: float) -> PerturbativeFamily:
    """Truth 0 on a single phenomenon, wrongness exactly a0*eps + a1*eps^2."""

    def coeff(n: int, _p: str) -> float:
        if n == 0:
            return a0
        if n == 1:
            return a1
        return 0.0

    return PerturbativeFamily(
        truth=lambda _p: 0.0,
        coeff=coeff,
        bound=abs(a0) + abs(a1),
        ratio=1.0,
        n_max=2,
        terminating=True,
    )


def geometric_family(bound: float, ratio: float) -> PerturbativeFamily:
    """A saturating family a_n(p) = B r^n (-1)^n, truth 0: the extreme case."""
    return PerturbativeFamily(
        truth=lambda _p: 0.0,
        coeff=lambda n, _p: bound * (ratio ** n) * (-1.0) ** n,
        bound=bound,
        ratio=ratio,
    )


def wilson_family() -> PerturbativeFamily:
    """Wilson's two-loop anomalous dimension eta(eps) = eps^2 / 54."""
    return binomial_family(0.0, 1.0 / 54.0)

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core objects
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class PerturbativeFamily:
    """A perturbative family of theories over a finite phenomenon set.

    Attributes
    ----------
    truth : mapping phenomenon -> exact value.
    coeff : coefficient function (n, p) -> a_n(p); the coefficient of
            eps^(n+1) in the wrongness series.
    bound : constant B with |a_n(p)| <= B r^n for all n, p.
    ratio : constant r (inverse radius of convergence).
    n_max : practical truncation used for numerically summing the series.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        truth: Callable[[str], float],
        coeff: Callable[[int, str], float],
        bound: float,
        ratio: float,
        n_max: int = 400,
        terminating: bool = False,
    ) -> None:
        if bound < 0.0 or ratio < 0.0:
            raise ValueError("bound and ratio must be nonnegative")
        self.truth = truth
        self.coeff = coeff
        self.bound = bound
        self.ratio = ratio
        self.n_max = n_max
        # A terminating series (finitely many nonzero coefficients) converges
        # for every coupling, so the disc-of-convergence guard is waived.
        self.terminating = terminating

    # -- series -----------------------------------------------------------

    def term(self, n: int, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """The n-th term a_n(p) eps^(n+1) of the wrongness series."""
        return self.coeff(n, p) * eps ** (n + 1)

    def wrongness(self, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """W(eps, p): the total deviation of the theory from the truth."""
        if not self.terminating and self.ratio * abs(eps) >= 1.0:
            raise ValueError("outside the disc of convergence: r|eps| >= 1")
        return math.fsum(self.term(n, eps, p) for n in range(self.n_max))

    def predict(self, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """The exact prediction truth(p) + W(eps, p)."""
        return self.truth(p) + self.wrongness(eps, p)

    def truncate(self, order: int, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """The order-N truncation: keep n < N, discard the rest."""
        return self.truth(p) + math.fsum(
            self.term(n, eps, p) for n in range(order)
        )

    def tail(self, order: int, eps: float, p: str) -> float:
        """R_N = W - sum_{n<N} w_n: exactly what the truncation throws away."""
        return self.wrongness(eps, p) - math.fsum(
            self.term(n, eps, p) for n in range(order)
        )

    # -- certified bounds and windows -------------------------------------

    def cauchy_bound(self, eps: float) -> float:
        """The uniform estimate B|eps| / (1 - r|eps|) on |W(eps, p)|."""
        denom = 1.0 - self.ratio * abs(eps)
        if denom <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError("outside the disc of convergence")
        return self.bound * abs(eps) / denom

    def meta_window(self, eta: float) -> float:
        """delta such that |eps| < delta implies |W(eps,p)| < eta for all p."""
        if eta <= 0.0:
            raise ValueError("threshold eta must be positive")
        return min(
            1.0 / (2.0 * (self.ratio + 1.0)),
            eta / (2.0 * (self.bound + 1.0)),
        )

    def hierarchy_window(self, m: int, n: int, p: str) -> float:
        """delta such that 0<|eps|<delta implies order-n beats order-m at p."""
        if not m < n:
            raise ValueError("require m < n")
        c = abs(self.coeff(m, p))
        if c == 0.0:
            raise ValueError("the m-th correction vanishes at p")
        noise = 2.0 * self.bound * (self.ratio ** n + self.ratio ** (m + 1)) + 1.0
        return min(1.0, 1.0 / (2.0 * (self.ratio + 1.0)), c / noise)


def pred_err(value: float, truth_value: float) -> float:
    """Pointwise prediction error |value - truth|."""
    return abs(value - truth_value)


def beats(value_a: float, value_b: float, truth_value: float) -> bool:
    """Does prediction a land strictly closer to the truth than b?"""
    return pred_err(value_a, truth_value) < pred_err(value_b, truth_value)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Concrete families
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def binomial_family(a0: float, a1: float) -> PerturbativeFamily:
    """Truth 0 on a single phenomenon, wrongness exactly a0*eps + a1*eps^2."""

    def coeff(n: int, _p: str) -> float:
        if n == 0:
            return a0
        if n == 1:
            return a1
        return 0.0

    return PerturbativeFamily(
        truth=lambda _p: 0.0,
        coeff=coeff,
        bound=abs(a0) + abs(a1),
        ratio=1.0,
        n_max=2,
        terminating=True,
    )


def geometric_family(bound: float, ratio: float) -> PerturbativeFamily:
    """A saturating family a_n(p) = B r^n (-1)^n, truth 0: the extreme case."""
    return PerturbativeFamily(
        truth=lambda _p: 0.0,
        coeff=lambda n, _p: bound * (ratio ** n) * (-1.0) ** n,
        bound=bound,
        ratio=ratio,
    )


def wilson_family() -> PerturbativeFamily:
    """Wilson's two-loop anomalous dimension eta(eps) = eps^2 / 54."""
    return binomial_family(0.0, 1.0 / 54.0)

def coefficients(n: int, p: str) -> float:
    """Corrections saturating |a_n(p)| <= B r^n with alternating signs.

    The phenomenon enters only through a bounded modulation, so the uniform
    Cauchy estimate holds with the same (B, r) at every phenomenon.
    """
    bound, ratio = 1.0, 2.0
    modulation = 0.40 + 0.15 * PHENOMENA.index(p)   # in (0, 1], so |a_n| <= B r^n

def wrongness(eps: float, p: str, n_max: int = 200) -> float:
    """W(eps, p) = sum_n a_n(p) eps^(n+1); converges for |eps| < 1/2."""
    total = 0.0
    for n in range(n_max):
        total += coefficients(n, p) * eps ** (n + 1)
    return total

    """delta = min{1/(2(r+1)), eta/(2(B+1))}."""
    return min(1.0 / (2.0 * (ratio + 1.0)), eta / (2.0 * (bound + 1.0)))

def meta_window(bound: float, ratio: float, eta: float) -> float:

    truth: Dict[str, float],

) -> List[str]:

    By the meta-theorem it suffices to locate the rival's bad set
    {p : |C(p) - t(p)| >= eta}; the approximate theory is guaranteed to win
    there for every coupling inside the window.

    Complexity: O(|Phi|) evaluations.
    """
    return [p for p in rival if abs(rival[p] - truth[p]) >= eta]


def audit_window(
    bound: float,
    ratio: float,
    eta: float,
    wrongness: "Tuple[float, ...] | None" = None,
) -> Tuple[float, str]:

    If actual wrongness values inside the window are supplied, the ratio of
    the largest observed |W| to eta measures the slack in the certificate.

    delta = meta_window(bound, ratio, eta)
    if not wrongness:
        return delta, "no observations supplied"
    worst = max(abs(w) for w in wrongness)
    return delta, f"worst observed |W| = {worst:.6g}, i.e. {worst / eta:.1%} of eta"

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, List


def hierarchy_window(
    bound: float,
    ratio: float,
    coeff_m: float,
    m: int,
    n: int,
) -> float:
    """Return delta guaranteeing that order n beats order m at the phenomenon.

    Parameters
    ----------
    bound   : B >= 0 from the uniform Cauchy estimate.
    ratio   : r >= 0 from the uniform Cauchy estimate.
    coeff_m : a_M(p), the first coefficient the coarse theory neglects;
              must be nonzero.
    m, n    : truncation orders with m < n.

    Returns
    -------
    delta = min{ 1, 1/(2(r+1)), c / (2B(r^n + r^(m+1)) + 1) },  c = |a_M(p)|.

    Complexity: O(log n) with fast exponentiation.

    Derivation.  The first two entries place the coupling in the half-disc
    r|eps| <= 1/2 and ensure |eps| < 1, so |eps|^(n+1) <= |eps|^(m+2).  The
    two-sided tail estimates then give
        |R_n| <= 2 B r^n |eps|^(m+2),
        |R_m| >= c |eps|^(m+1) - 2 B r^(m+1) |eps|^(m+2),
    and the third entry is exactly the inequality
        |eps| * 2B (r^n + r^(m+1)) < c
    that makes the first quantity smaller than the second.  Read as a ratio,
    delta is (signal: the first term the coarse theory neglects) divided by
    (noise: the geometric mass of what both theories neglect).
    """
    if not m < n:
        raise ValueError("require m < n")
    c = abs(coeff_m)
    if c == 0.0:
        raise ValueError("the m-th correction vanishes: no improvement guaranteed")
    noise = 2.0 * bound * (ratio ** n + ratio ** (m + 1)) + 1.0
    return min(1.0, 1.0 / (2.0 * (ratio + 1.0)), c / noise)


def chain_window(
    bound: float,
    ratio: float,
    coeff: Callable[[int], float],
    k: int,
) -> float:
    """A single window on which orders 0..k form a strict chain.

    Requires a_M(p) != 0 for every M < k.  Complexity: O(k log k).
    """
    windows: List[float] = [
        hierarchy_window(bound, ratio, coeff(m), m, m + 1) for m in range(k)
    ]
    return min(windows) if windows else 1.0


def optimal_order_asymptotic(ratio: float, eps: float) -> int:
    """Conjectural optimal truncation order for a factorially divergent family.

    For coefficients bounded only by |a_n| <= B n! r^n there is no radius of
    convergence and the chain must terminate.  The heuristic optimum sits where
    successive terms stop shrinking, at N* ~ 1/(r|eps|), with residual error of
    order exp(-1/(r|eps|)).  Included here as a computational conjecture, not a
    proved bound.
    """
    if ratio <= 0.0 or eps == 0.0:
        raise ValueError("require ratio > 0 and eps != 0")
    return max(1, int(round(1.0 / (ratio * abs(eps)))))

ALGORITHM TransitivityCounterexample(theories, truth)
  1. FOR each ordered triple (X, Y, Z) of distinct theories DO
  2.     IF X majority-beats Y and Y majority-beats Z
  3.        and NOT (X majority-beats Z) THEN RETURN (X, Y, Z)
  4. RETURN none",
      "code": """"Algorithm 3 -- Construction and Cycle Detection of the Empirical-Adequacy Tournament.

Predictive superiority is pointwise: theory X beats theory Y at phenomenon p if
|X(p) - t(p)| < |Y(p) - t(p)|.  Aggregating by majority over phenomena produces
a TOURNAMENT (a directed graph on theory-space), and that tournament may contain
cycles -- the Condorcet obstruction.  Consequently no scalar "closeness to
truth" can order theories consistently.

This module builds the tournament from error profiles and searches it for
cycles, certifying non-transitivity constructively.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import permutations
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Profile = Sequence[float]


def beats_at(x: float, y: float, truth: float) -> bool:
    """Does prediction x land strictly closer to the truth than y?"""
    return abs(x - truth) < abs(y - truth)


def majority_beats(x: Profile, y: Profile, truth: Profile) -> bool:
    """Does x beat y on a strict majority of the phenomena?"""
    if not (len(x) == len(y) == len(truth)):
        raise ValueError("profiles and truth must have equal length")
    wins = sum(1 for i in range(len(truth)) if beats_at(x[i], y[i], truth[i]))
    return 2 * wins > len(truth)


def build_tournament(
    theories: Dict[str, Profile], truth: Profile
) -> Dict[str, Set[str]]:
    """Adjacency map: name -> set of theories it majority-beats.

    Complexity: O(|theories|^2 * |Phi|).
    """
    return {
        a: {b for b in theories if b != a and majority_beats(theories[a], theories[b], truth)}
        for a in theories
    }


def find_cycle(graph: Dict[str, Set[str]]) -> List[str]:
    """Return a directed cycle as a list of vertices, or [] if acyclic.

    Iterative depth-first search with a colouring: white (unvisited), grey (on
    the current stack), black (finished).  A grey back-edge closes a cycle.

    Complexity: O(V + E).
    """
    colour: Dict[str, int] = {v: 0 for v in graph}
    parent: Dict[str, str] = {}

    for root in graph:
        if colour[root] != 0:
            continue
        stack: List[Tuple[str, bool]] = [(root, False)]
        while stack:
            v, finishing = stack.pop()
            if finishing:
                colour[v] = 2
                continue
            if colour[v] != 0:
                continue
            colour[v] = 1
            stack.append((v, True))
            for w in sorted(graph[v]):
                if colour[w] == 0:
                    parent[w] = v
                    stack.append((w, False))
                elif colour[w] == 1:
                    cycle = [v]
                    while cycle[-1] != w:
                        cycle.append(parent[cycle[-1]])
                    cycle.reverse()
                    return cycle
    return []


def transitivity_counterexample(
    theories: Dict[str, Profile], truth: Profile
) -> Tuple[str, str, str] | None:
    """Find (x, y, z) with x > y, y > z, but not x > z, if one exists.

    Complexity: O(|theories|^3 * |Phi|).
    """
    for x, y, z in permutations(theories, 3):
        if (
            majority_beats(theories[x], theories[y], truth)
            and majority_beats(theories[y], theories[z], truth)
            and not majority_beats(theories[x], theories[z], truth)
        ):
            return x, y, z
    return None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    truth: Profile = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
    theories: Dict[str, Profile] = {
        "A": (1.0, 2.0, 3.0),
        "B": (2.0, 3.0, 1.0),
        "C": (3.0, 1.0, 2.0),
    }
    graph = build_tournament(theories, truth)
    for name in sorted(graph):
        print(f"{name} majority-beats {sorted(graph[name])}")
    print("cycle found:", find_cycle(graph))
    print("transitivity counterexample:", transitivity_counterexample(theories, truth))

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def wrongness_geometric(eps: np.ndarray, ratio: float) -> np.ndarray:
    """Exact sum of a_n = (-ratio)^n: W(eps) = eps / (1 + ratio*eps)."""
    return eps / (1.0 + ratio * eps)


def truncation_geometric(eps: np.ndarray, ratio: float, order: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Partial sum sum_{n<order} (-ratio)^n eps^(n+1)."""
    out = np.zeros_like(eps)
    for n in range(order):
        out = out + ((-ratio) ** n) * eps ** (n + 1)
    return out


def hierarchy_window(bound: float, ratio: float, c: float, m: int, n: int) -> float:
    noise = 2.0 * bound * (ratio ** n + ratio ** (m + 1)) + 1.0
    return min(1.0, 1.0 / (2.0 * (ratio + 1.0)), c / noise)

            |ε|<δ, the approximate theory beats <em>every</em> rival
            on <em>every</em> phenomenon where the rival's error is at least η.
            The window is fixed before the rival is named.
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="view" id="v2">
        <div class="panel">
          <h2>Truncation error against the exact prediction</h2>
          <canvas id="cv2" width="1400" height="330"></canvas>
          <div class="readout">
            <div class="cell"><div class="k">chain window δ</div><div class="v" id="oD2">—</div></div>
            <div class="cell"><div class="k">inside the window?</div><div class="v" id="oIn">—</div></div>
          </div>
          <div class="verdict" id="verdict2">—</div>
          <table id="tbl"><thead><tr>
            <th>order N</th><th>truncated value</th><th>error |Rₙ|</th><th>vs previous</th>
          </tr></thead><tbody></tbody></table>
          <div class="formula">
            <b>The wrongness hierarchy theorem.</b> If the M-th correction is nonzero
            then for every N>M there is a punctured window
            0<|ε|<δ on which the order-N truncation strictly beats
            the order-M one, with
            δ = min{1, 1/(2(r+1)), |a<sub>M</sub>|/(2B(r<sup>N</sup>+r<sup>M+1</sup>)+1)}.
            Outside it, adding a correction can make things worse — try pushing
            ε up.
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
const st = {B:1, r:2, eps:0.005, eta:0.05, C:0.3, K:6, view:'v1'};

const W      = (B,r,e) => B*e/(1+r*e);
const term   = (B,r,e,n) => B*Math.pow(-r,n)*Math.pow(e,n+1);
const trunc  = (B,r,e,N) => {let s=0; for(let n=0;n<N;n++) s+=term(B,r,e,n); return s;};
const bound  = (B,r,e) => (r*e<1) ? B*e/(1-r*e) : Infinity;
const metaWin= (B,r,eta) => Math.min(1/(2*(r+1)), eta/(2*(B+1)));
const hierWin= (B,r,c,m,n) => Math.min(1, 1/(2*(r+1)),
                  c/(2*B*(Math.pow(r,n)+Math.pow(r,m+1))+1));
const chainWin=(B,r,K) => {let d=Infinity;
  for(let m=0;m<K;m++) d=Math.min(d,hierWin(B,r,Math.abs(B*Math.pow(r,m)),m,m+1));
  return d;};

function fmt(x,p=6){ if(!isFinite(x)) return '∞';
  return (Math.abs(x)<1e-4 && x!==0) ? x.toExponential(3) : x.toFixed(p); }

/* ---------- view 1: number line ---------- */
function draw1(){
  const cv=$('cv1'), g=cv.getContext('2d'), Wd=cv.width, Ht=cv.height;
  g.clearRect(0,0,Wd,Ht);
  const w   = W(st.B,st.r,st.eps);
  const eta = st.eta, C = st.C;
  const span = Math.max(Math.abs(C), eta, Math.abs(w))*1.35 + 0.02;
  const X = v => Wd/2 + (v/span)*(Wd/2-70);
  const yAx = Ht*0.60;

  // eta band around truth
  g.fillStyle='rgba(251,191,36,.10)';
  g.fillRect(X(-eta), 40, X(eta)-X(-eta), Ht-90);
  g.strokeStyle='rgba(251,191,36,.45)'; g.setLineDash([6,5]); g.lineWidth=2;
  [ -eta, eta ].forEach(v=>{g.beginPath();g.moveTo(X(v),40);g.lineTo(X(v),Ht-50);g.stroke();});
  g.setLineDash([]);
  g.fillStyle='#fbbf24'; g.font='16px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='center';
  g.fillText('threshold band  |error| < \u03b7', Wd/2, 30);

  // axis
  g.strokeStyle='#3d4d68'; g.lineWidth=2;
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(40,yAx); g.lineTo(Wd-40,yAx); g.stroke();

  const mark=(v,col,lab,dy)=>{
    const x=X(v);
    g.strokeStyle=col; g.lineWidth=3;
    g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(x,yAx-16); g.lineTo(x,yAx+16); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle=col; g.beginPath(); g.arc(x,yAx,7,0,7); g.fill();
    g.font='600 17px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='center';
    g.fillText(lab, x, yAx+dy);
  };
  mark(0,'#e8edf7','TRUTH  0', -34);
  mark(w,'#6ee7b7','approximate theory', 46);
  mark(C,'#f87171','rival C', 76);

  // error brackets
  g.font='15px sans-serif';
  g.strokeStyle='#6ee7b7'; g.lineWidth=2; g.setLineDash([3,4]);
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(0),yAx-52); g.lineTo(X(w),yAx-52); g.stroke();
  g.fillStyle='#6ee7b7'; g.textAlign='center';
  g.fillText('|W| = '+fmt(Math.abs(w),5), (X(0)+X(w))/2, yAx-60);
  g.strokeStyle='#f87171';
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(0),yAx+112); g.lineTo(X(C),yAx+112); g.stroke();
  g.fillStyle='#f87171';
  g.fillText('rival error = '+fmt(Math.abs(C),5), (X(0)+X(C))/2, yAx+132);
  g.setLineDash([]);

  const delta = metaWin(st.B,st.r,eta);
  const inWin = st.eps < delta;
  const covered = Math.abs(C) >= eta;
  const win = Math.abs(w) < Math.abs(C);

  $('oW').innerHTML = fmt(w,8);
  $('oB').innerHTML = fmt(bound(st.B,st.r,st.eps),8);
  $('oD').innerHTML = fmt(delta,8) + (inWin?' ✓ inside':' ✗ OUTSIDE');
  $('oC').innerHTML = fmt(Math.abs(C),8);

  const v=$('verdict1');
  if(inWin && covered){
    v.className='verdict v-ok';
    v.innerHTML = '<b>Guaranteed win.</b> The coupling is inside the window and the '+
      'rival\u2019s error reaches the threshold, so the meta-theorem certifies victory '+
      '\u2014 and indeed the approximate theory is closer to the truth'+
      (win?'':' (numerical check disagrees: report this!)')+'.';
  } else if(inWin && !covered){
    v.className='verdict v-warn';
    v.innerHTML = '<b>No claim made.</b> The rival\u2019s error ('+fmt(Math.abs(C),4)+
      ') is below the threshold \u03b7, so this phenomenon lies outside the certified '+
      'region. Observed outcome: the approximate theory '+(win?'still wins':'loses')+
      '. The theorem only ever claims victory on the rival\u2019s <em>bad set</em>.';
  } else {
    v.className = win ? 'verdict v-warn' : 'verdict v-bad';
    v.innerHTML = '<b>Outside the window.</b> \u03b5 = '+fmt(st.eps,4)+' exceeds \u03b4 = '+
      fmt(delta,4)+', so nothing is guaranteed. Observed outcome: the approximate theory '+
      (win?'happens to win anyway':'<b>LOSES to the crude rival</b> \u2014 exactly the '+
      'failure mode the sharpness counterexample exhibits at \u03b5 = 1/2')+'.';
  }
}

/* ---------- view 2: truncation tower ---------- */
function draw2(){
  const cv=$('cv2'), g=cv.getContext('2d'), Wd=cv.width, Ht=cv.height;
  g.clearRect(0,0,Wd,Ht);
  const K=st.K, exact=W(st.B,st.r,st.eps);
  const errs=[]; for(let N=0;N<=K;N++) errs.push(Math.abs(exact-trunc(st.B,st.r,st.eps,N)));
  const lo=Math.max(1e-18, Math.min(...errs.filter(e=>e>0))), hi=Math.max(...errs,1e-18);
  const L=40,Rr=40,T=30,Bm=52, pw=Wd-L-Rr, ph=Ht-T-Bm;
  const Y=e=>{const v=Math.max(e,lo*0.5);
    return T+ph*(1-(Math.log10(v)-Math.log10(lo*0.5))/(Math.log10(hi*2)-Math.log10(lo*0.5)));};
  // grid
  g.strokeStyle='#2c3a52'; g.lineWidth=1; g.font='13px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='right';
  for(let p=Math.ceil(Math.log10(lo*0.5)); p<=Math.floor(Math.log10(hi*2)); p++){
    const y=Y(Math.pow(10,p));
    g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(L,y); g.lineTo(Wd-Rr,y); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle='#6b7c99'; g.fillText('1e'+p, L-6, y+4);
  }
  const bw=pw/(K+1);
  for(let N=0;N<=K;N++){
    const x=L+N*bw+bw*0.22, w0=bw*0.56, y=Y(errs[N]);
    const worse = N>0 && errs[N]>=errs[N-1];
    g.fillStyle = worse ? 'rgba(248,113,113,.85)'
                        : 'rgba(110,231,183,'+(0.35+0.6*N/Math.max(1,K))+')';
    g.fillRect(x,y,w0,Ht-Bm-y);
    g.fillStyle='#e8edf7'; g.font='600 14px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='center';
    g.fillText('N='+N, x+w0/2, Ht-Bm+20);
    if(worse){ g.fillStyle='#f87171'; g.font='700 15px sans-serif';
               g.fillText('\u2191 worse', x+w0/2, y-8); }
  }
  g.fillStyle='#93a1bd'; g.font='14px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='left';
  g.fillText('error of the order-N truncation against the exact prediction (log scale)', L, 18);

  const dW=chainWin(st.B,st.r,K), inW=st.eps<dW && st.eps>0;
  $('oD2').innerHTML=fmt(dW,8);
  $('oIn').innerHTML= inW ? '<span style="color:#6ee7b7">yes</span>'
                          : '<span style="color:#f87171">no</span>';
  const anyWorse = errs.some((e,i)=>i>0 && e>=errs[i-1]);
  const v=$('verdict2');
  if(inW && !anyWorse){
    v.className='verdict v-ok';
    v.innerHTML='<b>Strict chain.</b> Inside the certified window every added correction '+
      'strictly reduces the error: the tower of knowingly-wrong truncations is totally '+
      'ordered by accuracy.';
  } else if(!inW && !anyWorse){
    v.className='verdict v-warn';
    v.innerHTML='<b>Outside the window, but still improving.</b> The window is sufficient, '+
      'not necessary \u2014 push \u03b5 further and the chain will eventually break.';
  } else {
    v.className='verdict v-bad';
    v.innerHTML='<b>The chain is broken.</b> At least one higher-order truncation is '+
      '<em>worse</em> than the one below it. \u201cHigher order is always better\u201d is '+
      'false outside the window \u2014 this is the sharpness counterexample in action.';
  }

  const tb=$('tbl').querySelector('tbody'); tb.innerHTML='';
  for(let N=0;N<=K;N++){
    const val=trunc(st.B,st.r,st.eps,N);
    const cmp = N===0 ? '—'
      : (errs[N]<errs[N-1] ? '<span class="down">▼ better</span>'
                           : '<span class="up">▲ worse</span>');
    tb.insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend',
      `<tr><td>${N}</td><td>${val.toPrecision(10)}</td><td>${errs[N].toExponential(4)}</td><td>${cmp}</td></tr>`);
  }
}

function render(){
  $('lB').textContent=st.B.toFixed(2); $('lR').textContent=st.r.toFixed(2);
  $('lE').textContent=st.eps.toFixed(4); $('lH').textContent=st.eta.toFixed(3);
  $('lC').textContent=st.C.toFixed(3);  $('lK').textContent=st.K;
  if(st.view==='v1') draw1(); else draw2();
}
[['B','B'],['R','r'],['E','eps'],['H','eta'],['C','C'],['K','K']].forEach(([id,key])=>{
  $(id).addEventListener('input',e=>{
    st[key] = (key==='K') ? parseInt(e.target.value,10) : parseFloat(e.target.value);
    render();
  });
});
document.querySelectorAll('.tab').forEach(t=>t.addEventListener('click',()=>{
  document.querySelectorAll('.tab').forEach(x=>x.classList.remove('on'));
  document.querySelectorAll('.view').forEach(x=>x.classList.remove('on'));
  t.classList.add('on'); $(t.dataset.view).classList.add('on'); st.view=t.dataset.view;
  $('rivalCtl').style.display = st.view==='v1' ? '' : 'none';
  $('ordCtl').style.display   = st.view==='v2' ? '' : 'none';
  render();
}));
render();
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    },
    {
      "title": "The Epistemic Arena: Drag the Truth, Build a Cycle",
      "description": "Two linked experiments on the structure of comparative adequacy. In the first, four theories -- labelled Aristotle, Newton, Einstein and Bohr -- make fixed numerical predictions on a strip, and the user clicks or drags to move the unknown truth along it. The strip is partitioned into coloured ownership bands, each an interval between consecutive midpoints, and live error chips crown the current winner. The outermost bands are marked unbounded, making the epistemic half-space theorem tangible: every theory that says anything owns an open, unbounded family of worlds, so predictive inferiority is never intrinsic to a theory but always a joint fact about theory and world. In the second experiment three theories carry editable error profiles over three phenomena, preloaded with the canonical rotation (1,2,3), (2,3,1), (3,1,2); a tournament graph is redrawn on every keystroke, with arrows meaning 'majority beats' and a live message that detects the three-cycle and explains why its presence rules out any consistent ranking of theories by closeness to the truth. Users can try to break the cycle, and discover how easily it comes back. Self-contained HTML, CSS and canvas JavaScript with no dependencies.",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8" />
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
<title>The Epistemic Arena</title>
<style>
  :root{
    --bg:#0f1420; --panel:#182031; --panel2:#1e2839; --ink:#e8edf7; --dim:#93a1bd;
    --accent:#a78bfa; --line:#2c3a52;
  }
  *{box-sizing:border-box}
  body{margin:0;background:var(--bg);color:var(--ink);
       font-family:-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;
       line-height:1.55}
  .wrap{max-width:1080px;margin:0 auto;padding:26px 20px 48px}
  h1{font-size:1.75rem;margin:0 0 6px;letter-spacing:-.02em}
  h1 span{color:var(--accent)}
  .sub{color:var(--dim);margin:0 0 22px;font-size:.97rem;max-width:76ch}
  .panel{background:var(--panel);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:14px;
         padding:16px 18px;margin-bottom:18px}
  .panel h2{font-size:.82rem;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.09em;color:var(--dim);
            margin:0 0 6px;font-weight:600}
  .panel p.note{color:var(--dim);font-size:.87rem;margin:0 0 12px}
  canvas{width:100%;display:block;border-radius:10px;background:var(--panel2);cursor:crosshair}
  .row{display:flex;gap:14px;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;margin-top:12px}
  .chip{background:var(--panel2);border:1px solid var(--line);border-radius:999px;
        padding:6px 14px;font-size:.86rem;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
  .chip b{color:var(--accent)}
  .win{border-color:rgba(167,139,250,.6);background:rgba(167,139,250,.14)}
  table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:.87rem;margin-top:8px;
        font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
  th,td{padding:7px 9px;border-bottom:1px solid var(--line);text-align:center}
  th{color:var(--dim);font-size:.74rem;text-transform:uppercase;letter-spacing:.06em}
  td:first-child,th:first-child{text-align:left}
  input[type=number]{width:74px;background:var(--panel2);border:1px solid var(--line);
    color:var(--ink);border-radius:7px;padding:5px 8px;font-size:.88rem;text-align:right}
  .cyc{margin-top:14px;padding:13px 15px;border-radius:11px;font-size:.92rem;
       background:rgba(167,139,250,.09);border:1px solid rgba(167,139,250,.42);color:#e4dbff}
  .no-cyc{background:rgba(96,165,250,.09);border-color:rgba(96,165,250,.42);color:#d6e6ff}
  code{font-family:ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,monospace;font-size:.86em;color:#c7b8ff}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Epistemic <span>Arena</span></h1>
  <p class="sub">
    Being right is not a property of a theory. It is a property of a theory
    <em>and the world it finds itself in</em> — and once you try to aggregate
    victories across many phenomena, the ranking can run in circles. Two
    experiments make both facts tangible.
  </p>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>Experiment 1 · Drag the truth</h2>
    <p class="note">
      Four theories predict fixed values. Click or drag anywhere on the strip to
      move the unknown truth <code>t</code>. Whichever theory is nearest wins that
      world. Every theory owns an open, unbounded region of worlds — that is the
      Epistemic Half-Space Theorem: for any two distinct predictions <code>a ≠ b</code>,
      the set <code>{t : |t−a| < |t−b|}</code> is exactly the half-line
      <code>(b−a)(2t−a−b) < 0</code>.
    </p>
    <canvas id="cvA" width="1400" height="300"></canvas>
    <div class="row" id="chips"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="panel">
    <h2>Experiment 2 · Build a Condorcet cycle</h2>
    <p class="note">
      Three theories, three phenomena, truth zero everywhere, so each entry <em>is</em>
      the error. Say <b>X majority-beats Y</b> if X is closer on at least two of the
      three. Edit the table and watch the tournament graph: the preloaded profiles
      <code>A=(1,2,3)</code>, <code>B=(2,3,1)</code>, <code>C=(3,1,2)</code> cycle, so
      majority empirical adequacy is not transitive and no consistent ranking of
      theories by “closeness to truth” exists.
    </p>
    <table id="tblP"><thead><tr>
      <th>theory</th><th>phenomenon 1</th><th>phenomenon 2</th><th>phenomenon 3</th>
    </tr></thead><tbody></tbody></table>
    <canvas id="cvB" width="1400" height="330" style="margin-top:14px;cursor:default"></canvas>
    <div class="cyc" id="cycMsg">—</div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
const $=id=>document.getElementById(id);

/* ============ Experiment 1 ============ */
const theories=[
  {n:'Aristotle', v:-3.2, c:'#f87171'},
  {n:'Newton',    v: 1.1, c:'#60a5fa'},
  {n:'Einstein',  v: 2.0, c:'#6ee7b7'},
  {n:'Bohr',      v: 5.4, c:'#fbbf24'}
];
let truth=0.4;
const LO=-8, HI=10;

function drawA(){
  const cv=$('cvA'), g=cv.getContext('2d'), Wd=cv.width, Ht=cv.height;
  g.clearRect(0,0,Wd,Ht);
  const L=50,R=50,pw=Wd-L-R, X=v=>L+(v-LO)/(HI-LO)*pw, yA=Ht*0.68;

  // ownership bands: nearest-neighbour cells (Voronoi on the line)
  const srt=[...theories].sort((a,b)=>a.v-b.v);
  for(let i=0;i<srt.length;i++){
    const lo = (i===0) ? LO : (srt[i-1].v+srt[i].v)/2;
    const hi = (i===srt.length-1) ? HI : (srt[i].v+srt[i+1].v)/2;
    g.fillStyle=srt[i].c+'22';
    g.fillRect(X(lo),40,X(hi)-X(lo),yA-70);
    g.strokeStyle=srt[i].c+'55'; g.setLineDash([4,5]); g.lineWidth=1.5;
    g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(X(hi),40); g.lineTo(X(hi),yA-30); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]);
    g.fillStyle=srt[i].c; g.font='600 14px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='center';
    g.fillText(srt[i].n+' wins here', (X(Math.max(lo,LO))+X(Math.min(hi,HI)))/2, 62);
  }
  g.fillStyle='#93a1bd'; g.font='13px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='left';
  g.fillText('\u2190 unbounded', L+6, yA-40);
  g.textAlign='right'; g.fillText('unbounded \u2192', Wd-R-6, yA-40);

  // axis + predictions
  g.strokeStyle='#3d4d68'; g.lineWidth=2;
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(L,yA); g.lineTo(Wd-R,yA); g.stroke();
  theories.forEach(t=>{
    const x=X(t.v);
    g.strokeStyle=t.c; g.lineWidth=3;
    g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(x,yA-13); g.lineTo(x,yA+13); g.stroke();
    g.fillStyle=t.c; g.beginPath(); g.arc(x,yA,6,0,7); g.fill();
    g.font='600 15px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='center';
    g.fillText(t.n, x, yA+34);
    g.font='13px sans-serif'; g.fillStyle='#93a1bd';
    g.fillText(t.v.toFixed(1), x, yA+52);
  });

  // truth marker
  const xt=X(truth);
  g.strokeStyle='#ffffff'; g.lineWidth=2.5; g.setLineDash([5,4]);
  g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(xt,40); g.lineTo(xt,yA+66); g.stroke(); g.setLineDash([]);
  g.fillStyle='#ffffff'; g.beginPath();
  g.moveTo(xt,yA-24); g.lineTo(xt-9,yA-40); g.lineTo(xt+9,yA-40); g.closePath(); g.fill();
  g.font='700 16px sans-serif'; g.textAlign='center'; g.fillStyle='#ffffff';
  g.fillText('the world  t = '+truth.toFixed(2), xt, yA-48);

  // error bars
  let best=null;
  theories.forEach(t=>{ const e=Math.abs(truth-t.v); if(!best||e<best.e) best={t,e}; });
  theories.forEach((t,i)=>{
    const e=Math.abs(truth-t.v), y=yA+82+i*0;
    g.strokeStyle=t.c; g.lineWidth=(t===best.t)?4:2; g.globalAlpha=(t===best.t)?1:.5;
    g.beginPath(); g.moveTo(xt,y+i*4); g.lineTo(X(t.v),y+i*4); g.stroke(); g.globalAlpha=1;
  });

  $('chips').innerHTML = theories.map(t=>{
    const e=Math.abs(truth-t.v), w=(t===best.t);
    return `<span class="chip ${w?'win':''}">${t.n}: error <b>${e.toFixed(3)}</b>${w?' ★ best':''}</span>`;
  }).join('');
}
function pick(ev){
  const cv=$('cvA'), rect=cv.getBoundingClientRect();
  const px=(ev.touches?ev.touches[0].clientX:ev.clientX)-rect.left;
  const s=cv.width/rect.width, L=50,R=50,pw=cv.width-L-R;
  truth = Math.max(LO, Math.min(HI, LO + (px*s-L)/pw*(HI-LO)));
  drawA();
}
let dragging=false;
$('cvA').addEventListener('mousedown',e=>{dragging=true;pick(e);});
window.addEventListener('mouseup',()=>dragging=false);
$('cvA').addEventListener('mousemove',e=>{if(dragging)pick(e);});
$('cvA').addEventListener('touchstart',e=>{pick(e);e.preventDefault();},{passive:false});
$('cvA').addEventListener('touchmove',e=>{pick(e);e.preventDefault();},{passive:false});

/* ============ Experiment 2 ============ */
const names=['A','B','C'];
const prof={A:[1,2,3], B:[2,3,1], C:[3,1,2]};

function buildTable(){
  const tb=$('tblP').querySelector('tbody'); tb.innerHTML='';
  names.forEach(n=>{
    const cells=prof[n].map((v,j)=>

### A guided tour of perturbation theory on theory-space

---

## 1. A puzzle worth taking seriously

Newton's law of gravitation is false. Spacetime is curved, gravity is not a force, and every physicist since 1915 has agreed on the point.

And every engineer since 1915 has used it anyway. Voyager flew past Neptune on a Newtonian trajectory. Tide tables are Newtonian. For most of the questions we actually ask, the false theory is not merely convenient — it is *more accurate in practice* than any competitor we can compute with.

This is not an embarrassment about Newton. It happens everywhere:

| Theory | Verdict | Still used for |
|---|---|---|
| Newtonian gravitation | False since 1915 | Spacecraft navigation, tides, orbital mechanics |
| The Bohr atom | False since 1926 | Hydrogen spectral lines to four digits |
| The ideal gas law | Never exactly true | Refrigeration, meteorology, engine design |
| Any truncated loop expansion | Wrong *by construction* | Essentially all quantitative predictions of the Standard Model |

By the end of this page you will have a theorem that explains the pattern, a second theorem that explains why "compute one more order" is a rational thing to do, and — just as importantly — two explicit counterexamples showing exactly where both explanations stop working.

> **The question in one line.** Can we prove that an *approximately correct* theory must outpredict its rivals — and if so, on which phenomena, against which rivals, and under what conditions?

---

## 2. Stripping a theory down to its skeleton

Forget ontology. Empirically, a physical theory does one thing: it assigns numbers to measurable situations.

- A set $\Phi$ of **phenomena** — the perihelion shift of Mercury, the boiling point of water at altitude, the electron's magnetic moment.
- A **theory** is a function $T : \Phi \to \mathbb{R}$.
- Somewhere out there is the **truth**, another function $t : \Phi \to \mathbb{R}$, which we never see.
- The **error** at a phenomenon is $E(T,p) = |T(p) - t(p)|$.
- We say $T$ **beats** $C$ at $p$ when $E(T,p) < E(C,p)$.

Notice how little this says. Not that $T$ is true. Not that $T$ is beautiful. Just: at *this* phenomenon, it lands closer. Superiority is comparative, local, and nothing more. Everything below flows from taking that austerity seriously.

<details>
<summary><b>Why be this minimal? (click to expand)</b></summary>

Richer accounts of theories — as sets of models, as axiom systems, as research programmes — are indispensable for questions about explanation and unification. But they smuggle in structure that predictive-accuracy questions do not need, and that structure tends to obscure the quantifiers. The whole force of the main theorem lies in the *order* in which "for all rivals", "for all phenomena", and "there exists a window" appear. A minimal setting makes that order visible. See the [Stanford Encyclopedia entry on scientific realism](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/scientific-realism/) for the richer accounts this deliberately sets aside.

</details>

---

## 3. Wrongness is a series, not a verdict

Here is the modelling move that makes the whole subject go. Almost every successful approximate theory is the leading part of an expansion in something small: $v/c$ in relativity, $\hbar$ in the semiclassical limit, the fine-structure constant in electrodynamics, $\varepsilon = 4-d$ in critical phenomena.

So define a **perturbative family of theories**: a truth function together with correction coefficients $a_n(p)$, giving for each coupling $\varepsilon$ the prediction

$$T_\varepsilon(p) \;=\; t(p) \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n(p)\,\varepsilon^{\,n+1}}_{\text{the wrongness } W(\varepsilon,p)}$$

subject to one condition — a **uniform Cauchy bound**

$$|a_n(p)| \;\le\; B\,r^{\,n} \qquad \text{for every } n \text{ and every } p.$$

The corrections grow no faster than geometrically, and — this is the load-bearing word — *uniformly across all phenomena at once*.

> **Theorem (Convergent Wrongness).** If $r|\varepsilon| < 1$ then the wrongness series converges absolutely and
> $$|W(\varepsilon,p)| \;\le\; \frac{B|\varepsilon|}{1 - r|\varepsilon|}$$
> for every phenomenon $p$ simultaneously.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof (two lines)</b></summary>

Each term obeys $|a_n(p)\varepsilon^{n+1}| \le B r^n |\varepsilon|^{n+1} = (B|\varepsilon|)(r|\varepsilon|)^n$. Summing the geometric majorant gives $B|\varepsilon|/(1-r|\varepsilon|)$, and the triangle inequality for absolutely convergent series transfers the bound to $|W|$. $\blacksquare$

The point is not the difficulty; it is that the right-hand side contains **no $p$**. Shrink the coupling and the theory becomes accurate *everywhere at once*.

</details>

Equivalently: for every tolerance $\eta > 0$ there is a window $|\varepsilon| < \delta$ inside which $|W(\varepsilon,p)| < \eta$ for all $p$, and one may take

$$\delta \;=\; \min\left\{\frac{1}{2(r+1)},\ \frac{\eta}{2(B+1)}\right\}.$$

That formula is not decoration. It is computable, and the first algorithm below implements it.

{{algorithm:0}}

## 4. The meta-theorem

Now the payoff. Fix an approximately correct theory and an accuracy threshold $\eta > 0$.

> **Theorem (Unreasonable Effectiveness of Wrong Theories).** There is a $\delta > 0$ such that for every coupling with $|\varepsilon| < \delta$, for **every rival theory $C$ whatsoever**, and for every phenomenon $p$ at which $C$'s error is at least $\eta$, the theory $T_\varepsilon$ beats $C$ at $p$.

Read the quantifiers slowly, because they carry the entire content.

- $\delta$ is chosen **first**, from $B$, $r$ and $\eta$ alone.
- It does **not** depend on the rival. Not on Aristotelian physics, not on a neural network, not on a rival unification programme, not on the true theory implemented with a bug.
- It does **not** depend on the phenomenon.

The proof, once the convergence estimate is in hand, is a single line: $E(T_\varepsilon,p) = |W(\varepsilon,p)| < \eta \le E(C,p)$. Trivial as mathematics; substantial as epistemology.

Time to get your hands on it. In the laboratory below, the first tab puts the truth at $0$, places your approximate theory and a rival on the number line, and shades the threshold band. Start inside the window and try to defeat the theorem with any rival you like; then push $\varepsilon$ up and watch the guarantee dissolve.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

**Three things to try.**
1. Slide the rival anywhere. As long as its error reaches $\eta$, you cannot beat the approximate theory — that is the theorem.
2. Slide the rival *inside* the threshold band. The verdict panel turns amber: no claim is made there. The theorem only ever promises victory on the rival's **bad set**.
3. Push $\varepsilon$ past $\delta$. Now a crude constant can win. Hold that thought — §7 turns it into a theorem.

<details>
<summary><b>What the meta-theorem does <i>not</i> say</b></summary>

It does not say $T_\varepsilon$ is true — generically its wrongness is nonzero and it is false at every phenomenon. It does not say $T_\varepsilon$ beats $C$ everywhere — where $C$ happens to be very accurate, $C$ may well win. It says exactly this: *the region of the rival's badness is a region of the approximate theory's comparative goodness*, and that region is specified by a condition anyone can check without evaluating the approximate theory at all.

</details>

Two corollaries make it bite.

**The superiority region is never empty.** If a rival is inexact at even one phenomenon $p_0$, take $\eta = E(C,p_0) > 0$ and the theorem hands you a window on which $p_0$ belongs to the superiority region.

**And imperfection is generic.** Over a countable phenomenon space, given any theory and any $\delta > 0$, there is a shift $0 < c < \delta$ making the shifted theory wrong at *every single phenomenon*.

<details>
<summary><b>The cardinality trick behind genericity</b></summary>

The "bad" shifts — those that accidentally hit the truth somewhere — form the set $\{t(p) - T(p) : p \in \Phi\}$, the image of a countable set, hence countable. The interval $(0,\delta)$ has the cardinality of the continuum. So almost every tiny shift misses the truth everywhere. Nowhere-exact theories are *dense* in theory-space: "your rival is imperfect somewhere" is not a caveat, it is the typical case.

</details>

## 5. The tower of deliberate lies

Nobody sums an infinite perturbation series. What one computes is a **truncation** — keep the first $N$ corrections, bin the rest:

$$T^{(N)}_\varepsilon(p) \;=\; t(p) + \sum_{n<N} a_n(p)\,\varepsilon^{\,n+1}.$$

This is a knowingly wrong theory in the purest sense: its author can name the terms being discarded. The discarded remainder is the **tail** $R_N$, and it obeys an exact recursion that is the engine of everything in this section:

$$R_N \;=\; \underbrace{a_N\varepsilon^{N+1}}_{\text{first neglected term}} \;+\; R_{N+1}.$$

The error of a truncation is its first neglected term plus the error of the next truncation down the line. Squeeze this between matched upper and lower bounds and you get:

> **Theorem (Wrongness Hierarchy).** Let $p$ be a phenomenon at which the $M$-th correction does not vanish, and let $N > M$. Then there is a punctured window $0 < |\varepsilon| < \delta$ on which the $N$-th order truncation **strictly beats** the $M$-th.
>
> Moreover a single window serves all of orders $0,1,\dots,K$ at once: on it, the truncations are **totally ordered** by accuracy.

<details>
<summary><b>The two-sided estimates, and where $\delta$ comes from</b></summary>

In the half-disc $r|\varepsilon| \le 1/2$,

$$|a_N(p)||\varepsilon|^{N+1} - 2Br^{N+1}|\varepsilon|^{N+2} \;\le\; |R_N| \;\le\; 2Br^{N}|\varepsilon|^{N+1}.$$

The upper bound is the geometric majorant. The lower bound comes from the recursion: $|a_N\varepsilon^{N+1}| = |R_N - R_{N+1}| \le |R_N| + |R_{N+1}|$, then apply the upper bound at order $N+1$. The gap between them is a full power of $\varepsilon$ — exactly the room needed to conclude. The resulting window is

$$\delta \;=\; \min\left\{1,\ \frac{1}{2(r+1)},\ \frac{|a_M(p)|}{2B(r^N + r^{M+1}) + 1}\right\},$$

which reads as a **signal-to-noise ratio**: the first term the coarse theory neglects, divided by the geometric mass of everything both theories neglect. Improvement happens exactly while the newly captured term outweighs everything still missing.

</details>

This is the precise sense in which the wrongness of a theory "forms a convergent series toward truth". Not just that the limit is right — that the *sequence of deliberate falsehoods is strictly, monotonically improving*. The tower of lies is a ladder, and each rung is closer to the sky than the last. When a physicist says "we went to three loops and the agreement improved", this is the theorem being relied on.

## 6. Being right is a fact about the *world*

Two results now reframe what "closer to the truth" can even mean.

Suppose two theories predict $a \ne b$ at some phenomenon. In which possible worlds — which values $t$ of the unknown truth — does the first beat the second? One line of algebra:

$$|t - a| < |t - b| \iff (b-a)(2t - a - b) < 0,$$

a **half-line** in $t$.

> **Theorem (Epistemic Half-Space).** For any two distinct predictions, the set of worlds in which the first outpredicts the second is a nonempty, open, unbounded half-line. It always contains the world $t = a$ where the first theory is exactly right, and it stretches to infinity.

No prediction is unconditionally inferior. Every theory that says *anything* is the best available theory in an unbounded family of worlds.

And a bracing companion bound, true whatever the truth is:

$$|T(p) - C(p)| \;\le\; E(T,p) + E(C,p).$$

**Disagreement forces error.** If two theories differ by $D$ at a phenomenon, at least one of them is wrong by at least $D/2$. Controversy is a truth-independent lower bound on collective ignorance.

## 7. Why you cannot simply rank theories

If superiority is local, the natural repair is to aggregate: declare $X$ better than $Y$ if $X$ beats $Y$ on *most* phenomena. This fails — and it fails in the way democracies fail.

Three phenomena with truth $0$, and three theories with error profiles

$$A = (1,2,3), \qquad B = (2,3,1), \qquad C = (3,1,2).$$

Then $A$ beats $B$ on phenomena 1 and 2; $B$ beats $C$ on 1 and 3; $C$ beats $A$ on 2 and 3. Every one a two-out-of-three majority. But $A$ beats $C$ on phenomenon 1 only. Majority empirical adequacy runs in a **Condorcet cycle** and is not transitive.

The second experiment in the arena above lets you edit the profiles and watch the tournament graph rewire itself in real time. Try to break the cycle; then try to build a new one.

<details>
<summary><b>Why this is an Arrow-type obstruction, and what to do about it</b></summary>

Any aggregation of pointwise errors into a total order on theory-space must break either transitivity or the independence of the individual phenomena — the same trilemma [Arrow's impossibility theorem](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/arrows-theorem/) forces on voting rules. The constructive response is to stop looking for an order. Comparative adequacy is a **tournament**: a directed graph on theory-space, cycles permitted.

Note how the meta-theorem escapes the obstruction: it never aggregates. It compares one theory to one rival at one phenomenon, and specifies the winning region by an explicit, checkable condition on the rival.

</details>
